227.s: On the second day Mandel recalls a year or two of study with Wolpe around 1951, learning atonal writing, and says he learns better by experience than formal schooling.
227.ch: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
227.q: Well, it didn't actually, it really didn't not because – Stefan Wolpe was wonderful but I wasn't with him long enough to have him make a large – I moved from New York very quickly after I started studying with him. So, it wasn't really, you know a pivotal thing, like I was with him a year or two…

227.s: Mandel praises George Tremblay, who taught many film writers a sensual Berg-like approach to atonality.
227.ch: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
227.q: David Raksin did. Oh, he’s wonderful, he was wonderful and he understood a lot, he understood about jazz, he understood about all types of music, even though he was strictly a classicist himself he was not all in the tradition. And he wrote gorgeous music that was atonal but tonal, you know it was…

148.t: Later meeting with Copland and leaving his lessons
148.s: He met Copland years later at a Brooklyn Museum concert, reflects on whether Copland was serious as a teacher, and recalls quitting.
148.q: I attended a concert that he gave at the Brooklyn Museum, the museum on Eastern Parkway. He gave a concert there and I went up to him after the concert and said hello. He remembered me and smiled and shook my hand.

148.s: His mother found Copland for him; Copland only asked for melodies and gave his opinions, so Handy wrote them on the train to lessons.
148.q: He was known to be a great composer in those days, but I don't think he was very secure financially. Of course I only judge by where he was living, where he was teaching, the kind of surroundings he had. Even that was not a good experience. He didn't give me anything but opinions.

687.s: He had teachers briefly but learned mostly from experience.
687.q: yes I've had teachers from time to time but actually I never was in one place long enough to derive a whole lot but I got the the pointers and the information that I wanted most of mine has come from from experience I've had oodles and oodles of that

848.s: Kimball's schoolmate and teacher Valmo Victor, who taught many New Orleans musicians.
848.q: I'm sure that he is. I'm sure that he is. He's responsible for many musicians, many good musicians. Lord Jack Willis that plays trumpet, he taught him to play music. Al Goodman, the bass player, you've heard of him? Heard of him, yeah. He's a very fine bass player. Another fellow that they called…

601.t: No bands from the plantations below Magnolia; Jim Humphrey teaching there
601.s: Asked about Magnolia plantation, home of Chris Kelly and Jim Robinson, Martin says no bands came from there but Jim Humphrey went down to teach and Governor Warmoth hired a professor. A barber who played baritone came from there.
601.q: They didn't have no bands come from down there. You didn't hear any musicians from down there. They didn't, the old man uh... See they were down there on the plantation. Deer Range. Deer Range. Yeah. And you take uh... You take old man... Uh... Ulfrey. Used to go down to teach him. Yeah, Jim…

199.s: Hogan taught Hanon exercises and two-part inventions to a small class.
199.q: Well I know that one time he had three of us, he had his niece, he had another guy, myself, we had a class, we all were like on the same category, playing music, we were all about the same level. He was playing Hanan exercises and he had us playing, I got one or two part inventions with him. Yeah.…

211.t: Meeting Schoenberg and the Stoloff circle in Hollywood
211.s: Through Morris Stoloff's house he met Ernst Toch and Schoenberg, who told of arranging for Radio Berlin.
211.q: Schoenberg — after the war Arnold Schoenberg was in Hollywood. He was somewhat of a refugee, not politically but musically. You know he was lost in Germany and Austria. It was a bad time to go back. And he had friends. There was a man by the name of Morris Stoloff who was music director at Columbia…

1036.t: A woman arranger's teachers and atonality in school
1036.s: They discuss an arranger who studied with Rayburn Wright, Bob Brookmeyer and Gil Evans and was laughed at for writing in a key.
1036.ch: Arranging craft, ownership and the business
1036.q: Yeah. She studied with Rayburn Wright, who I also studied with, but I think she really found her groove when she studied with Bobby Brookmeyer and Gil Evans, when she started listening to them and studying with them. That really helped her a lot. And I think it reinforced her whole body of work.…

749.t: Taking original songs to Brewster, and his limits with jazz charts
749.s: She cannot recall bringing songs; later in New York she studied again with Brewster and found he did not know jazz chord jargon.
749.q: Oh gosh, oh my God you’re asking me — that’s okay. I don’t remember but I do recall at some point — oh no that was in my New York days because Dr. Brewster moved to New York three years after I moved to New York and I picked up my studies again with him.

492.t: Halsey Stevens's side lessons and the Vedanta nun
492.s: Lloyd recalls Stevens telling him to keep hearing what he hears despite USC rules, and a Vedanta nun asking if meditation changed his character.
492.ch: Higgins, Hendrix and the spiritual path
492.q: Well the spirituality of it was, you know. Because I’d heard that stuff and it’s like that whole thing you brought out about Bartok. I didn’t formally study with Halsey Stevens, he took me on the side and said, “Listen man, here’s what’s happenin’, and keep going with what you’re doing.” He’d look…

104.t: Studies and composition exercises at the Guildhall
104.s: She studied about three years of solo piano, Bach, Beethoven and Chopin and wrote short pieces under a didactic teacher.
104.ch: Jazz records, vaudeville and starting out
104.q: I never did that. I never did that. It was always . . . Maybe I would have if I had stayed longer. I never got to the point of playing a concerto. I was doing a lot of Bach and Beethoven and . . .

64.s: He praises Moore, who shielded him from the department head, let him practice jazz, and steered him toward Ravel, Debussy and Ellington.
64.q: Well the first, when I first went to Virginia State she was the harmony and theory teacher, Jay Harold Montay was the head of the department and he was a pianist and piano teacher and the choral director. So she was a much more open and much more… I say this out of sheer prejudice, a much better…

113.t: Dr. Boubendorf, the strict German teacher who asked him to play
113.s: His strict German teacher Dr. Boubendorf corrected his habits, then heard him playing his own pieces and had him play for the class.
113.q: B-o-u-b-e-n-d-o-r-f. Boubendorf. And he was real strict in his teaching. You might say, oh, well, -- like, phrases that we would use, and he'd straighten you out right quick. No, that's so-and-so. You don't call that a this or this, you call that so-and-so. He was very, very, very staunch and…

453.t: Four years of lessons with Eddie Hudson and what he taught
453.s: Randolph studied Goodrich's Analysis of Music with Hudson, passed this on to his pupils, and recalls Hudson's advice about not forming habits you cannot do without.
453.q: Eddie for about four years. I took harmony, theory of harmony then, Goodrich Analysis of Music -- now, there's where you learn something about music. Then -- and I passed -- I used that with my pupils too. A lot of the information I got out of the books with Eddie Hudson, such things like -- now,…

93.t: Chuckles as teacher and straight man
93.s: J. D. explained steps and Green demonstrated them, which Powell liked; Green was the outgoing one and J. D. the cool straight man.
93.ch: Billy Pierce Studio and New York tap
93.q: great tap dancer, see, because I could ask him a question. He would sit down and explain to me, and he would ask -- he would tell me, say, 'Now try; see how you like it,' you know. If I would do it correctly, he would sit there. If I'd do it incorrectly, he would get up and show me how to do it…

387.s: Teachers were a crutch and an intellectual force.
387.q: : It's being lead into some strange direction you never really thought was there, and you found it worked for you. I never really learned anything from teachers, it's just that they were a crutch, a necessary crutch at the time, at least with me (inaudible). I never really learned anything from him…

389.s: Lessons were mathematical, rhythm first, and after about two and a half years Schillinger died.
389.q: [That opened] up, and he had a long, drawn out course which is mostly mathematical, but it's wonderful, really. And you -- for six months to a year you had to stick on just rhythm.

7.t: Timothy's method: counterpoint and the three progressions
7.s: Thomas credits Timothy, a Schillinger pupil, for teaching counterpoint in six weeks and a mathematical view of progressions and the cycle of fifths.
7.q: And I didn't have the privilege of studying with Schillinger. I guess I wasn't ready to study with Schillinger anyway, when he was in town. But I studied from
